beats.narration_text: Hi — I'm Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI. In 2020, two researchers built a thought experiment starring a lonely octopus. Ever since, people have been calling it "the Chinese Room, rebuilt for AI." Here's a two-question game that shows that's not quite right.

props.artifactHeading: the octopus test isn't what you think
artifactLines: Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI.
In 2020, two researchers built a thought experiment starring a lonely octopus.
Everyone calls it “the Chinese Room, rebuilt for AI.” Here's a two-question game that shows that's not quite right.

beats.narration_text: Here's a game before I answer it for you. Two questions — one is Searle's, one is Bender and Koller's. See if you can tell which is which before I say. Question one: can a machine that just follows rules ever actually be thinking, no matter where the rules came from? Question two: can meaning be learned from nothing but form, with no other input at all? ...Which one is Searle's?

artifactLines: Question one: can a machine that just follows rules ever actually be thinking — no matter where the rules came from?
Question two: can meaning be learned from nothing but form, with no other input at all?

beats.factcheck_ref: FACTCHECK.md 1.4, 3.2 — restated as a guessing game, no new claims

beats.narration_text: Question one is Searle's, from 1980. Question two is Bender and Koller's, forty years later. And here's the part the retelling skips: close readers of their paper are explicit that this is not the Chinese Room again. Two different questions, wearing very similar costumes.

artifactLines: Question one — Searle, 1980. Question two — Bender & Koller, 2020.
Two different questions, wearing very similar costumes.

beats.narration_text: And here's the detail almost nobody mentions, the one that made me sit up: Harnad is on the list. The exact embodiment fix Searle's paper had already rejected — sensors, a body, a way to touch the world — is the fix Harnad is proposing. Same room. Same rejected reply. Just a different person, a decade later, betting that Searle got it wrong.

artifactLines: Searle's paper already rejected the embodiment fix — sensors, a body, a way to touch the world.
Harnad proposes exactly that fix, a decade later.
Same room. Same rejected reply. A different bet on who was wrong.

beats.narration_text: That's two turns of a four-part story. There's one more — Bender publicly correcting how her own famous term gets used, five years after she coined it. All four, in the full video. Watch 'Same Room, Different Argument' for the whole thing — the link's right below.
